content: Multiple Micronutrient Supplements (MMS) have been shown to be highly cost-effective when compared to Iron and Folic Acid (IFA) supplements, based on data modeled by Nutrition International using estimates from the World Health Organization (WHO) analysis. The cost-effectiveness analysis assumed that 30% of pregnant women received 180 days of supplementation, with costs and benefits calculated over a 10-year period. The cost estimates were derived from UNICEF Supply Catalogue pricing (2016). The primary analysis utilized statistically significant estimates of low birth weight and small-for-gestational-age (SGA) outcomes from the WHO meta-analysis. MMS remained highly cost-effective across all scenarios. When the iron dose was considered, transitioning from 30 mg IFA supplements to MMS was still very cost-effective, even when non-statistically significant effects were included. However, transitioning from 60 mg IFA supplements to MMS was not cost-effective when non-statistically significant outcomes were included, primarily due to the impact of neonatal mortality estimates in this comparison. These findings should be interpreted with caution. The actual supply costs of MMS may be lower than current estimates and are expected to decrease with increased global production and distribution. Apart from the cost of the supplements themselves, other costs, such as facility and program costs, would likely remain the same for both MMS and IFA supplements. However, there would be additional transition costs, including retraining staff, designing new teaching materials, updating guidelines, and administrative expenses. The supply costs of MMS are estimated to be approximately double those of IFA supplements. The certainty of evidence regarding these costs is considered moderate, as the supply costs are based on UNICEF Supply Catalogue data. Other costs, apart from transition costs, are expected to be similar between MMS and IFA. Equity considerations indicate that disadvantaged populations, such as women who are poor, less educated, or living in rural areas, often have lower health intervention coverage and worse health outcomes compared to more advantaged women in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). Effective interventions to improve the nutritional status of pregnant women and adolescent girls in LMICs could help address maternal and neonatal health inequalities by improving general health and preventing maternal illnesses related to vitamin and mineral deficiencies. Switching from IFA supplements to MMS is likely to be acceptable to key stakeholders. Women generally value antenatal care (ANC) as a source of knowledge and appreciate advice that promotes a healthy pregnancy and baby. Health professionals are generally supportive of providing pregnancy-related nutritional advice but may feel constrained by a lack of training, resources, and time. If women are not required to pay for supplements, MMS is likely to be as acceptable as IFA supplements. MMS may also be more acceptable in settings where IFA supplementation involves taking multiple tablets or where MMS with 30 mg iron is associated with fewer gastrointestinal side effects compared to higher-dose IFA supplements. The feasibility of implementing MMS supplementation depends on ensuring the availability and affordability of MMS. In LMIC settings, a lack of resources, including the availability of supplements and trained staff, may limit the implementation of MMS programs. However, if MMS is provided free of charge and is readily available, it should be as feasible to implement as IFA supplementation. The updated global guideline on MMS will be disseminated online and in print, with translations into six UN languages. The recommendation will be reviewed and updated as new evidence becomes available. WHO will prioritize its independent normative guidance based on strategic shifts outlined in its Constitution and the Thirteenth General Programme of Work (2019–2023). All technical products developed during the recommendation process will be archived for future reference and use.
